And powers come back: if the lengths are multiplied by $k$, the areas are multiplied by $k^2$, just as when going from metres to square centimetres. Thales' theorem, at the end, is a rule of three with a picture.

Áreas y volúmenes: el error clásico: Areas and volumes: the classic mistake
Aquí está el error más repetido de toda: Here is the most repeated mistake in all of geometry, and it is worth making it once deliberately so as never to make it again. If you double all the lengths of a figure, the area does not double: it is multiplied by four. And the volume, by eight.
Compruébalo con la figura más tonta que: Check it with the silliest figure there is. Take a square of side 1 cm: its area is 1 cm². Double the side to 2 cm: the area becomes $2\times 2 = 4$ cm². You have played no tricks, and the area has been multiplied by four. The reason is visible if you draw it: four of the small squares fit in the big one, two across by two up.
Con el volumen ocurre lo mismo una dimen: The same happens with volume one dimension higher: in a cube of double the side, two fit across, two along and two up, that is, eight little cubes. And since any figure can be imagined filled with little squares or little cubes, what holds for the square holds for any shape, however odd.
La regla general se recuerda por el <str: The general rule is remembered by the exponent, which matches the number of dimensions of what you are measuring: a length has one dimension and goes with $k$, an area has two and goes with $k^2$, a volume has three and goes with $k^3$.

With $k=3$, for instance: the sides become 3 times bigger, the surfaces 9 times and the capacities 27 times. That is why a 1:3 scale model does not need a third of the material, but twenty-seven times less.

La razón de semejanza es $\\frac{1}{2}$: The scale factor is $\frac{1}{2}$ and the area is multiplied by $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}$: the small one is a quarter of the big one.
No hay ninguna cuenta que dé tres cuarto: No calculation gives three quarters. The area goes with the square of the factor: a quarter.
Esto tiene consecuencias que van mucho m: This has consequences going far beyond geometry. An animal twice as tall weighs eight times as much, but the cross-section of its bones is only four times greater: that is why elephants have thick legs and ants do not. It is called the square-cube law, and Galileo stated it in 1638.
Esa misma ley decide cosas muy alejadas: That same law decides things far removed from animals. A small body has a lot of surface for little volume, and so crushed ice cools a drink far faster than one big cube, kindling catches before a log does and a hummingbird has to eat almost without stopping: it loses heat through an enormous surface relative to its weight. In cooking it is why potato cut small browns and cut large stays raw inside.
En ingeniería el cuadrado-cubo es una re: In engineering the square-cube law is a design constraint. Doubling the size of a drone multiplies its weight by eight and the area of its rotors only by four, so the whole system has to be redesigned rather than simply “made bigger”. The same limits the height of buildings and the size of ships, and explains why chemical reactors that work in the laboratory sometimes fail when scaled up to a factory: heat is generated by the volume and carried away by the surface, and as the vessel grows that sum stops working out.
